rv.q: Like the prior stagings, “Philadelphia,” directed by Ciarán O’Reilly—who also portrays Gar’s taciturn father, S.B.—is acted with luminous grace, digging into the ripe comedy but also underscoring the tenderness suffusing Friel’s writing.

What the long throw of time makes clear is that its writer was distinctive, compelling, and humane, an expansive soul with sharp, clear eyes and restless feet, looking for his way of being in the world.
And happily, the Irish Rep production helmed by Ciarán O’Reilly captures the great play in all its tragicomic glory.
I doubt that message has often come across more powerfully than it does here.
Those fond of Brian Friel’s plays will find many good reasons here to sing out, Irish Repertory, here I come!
The stellar performances of McElwee and Shively, playing off each other, more than suffice to make this revival compulsory viewing.
As it continues, "Philadelphia" gets better and better.
If you don’t know Philadelphia, Here I Come!, this Irish Rep production offers a solid way to acquaint yourself with Friel’s lightly inventive, quietly devastating play.

Few playwrights have captured the competing urge to break out of stifling circumstances while desperately clinging to the hope that love might yet be found there, even as the hour of departure approaches.
Friel's play is pleasant and atmospheric, but it remains rather slight.
In this flawlessly cast version, it’s a joy to report how successful an evening in the theater this is.

Philadelphia, Here I Come! at the Irish Repertory Theatre is truly fantastic in its ability to evoke all of these profound cultural questions and its comfort exploring them through these juxtapositions of characters who are very much parallel existences of each other.
It’s a fulfilling evening of theatre all the way around and worth your time beyond the opportunity to see Brian Friel’s work.

The 1964 drama put Friel on the map, and it’s easy to see the appeal of this domestic drama set in a small Irish community in 1962 where everybody knows each other and therefore things are often left unsaid, even when it’s too late.

cn.t: Irish Rep's revival of Friel's 1964 breakthrough earns strong praise, with critics particularly lauding the dual-actor portrayal of protagonist Gar's public and private selves as a compelling theatrical device in this melancholy yet affecting emigration tale.
